strengths: Introduces a clear, well-motivated, and easily interpretable metric (two-sample classifier test) for quantifying distributional symmetry breaking in datasets, sidestepping the need for a domain-specific kernel required by prior MMD-based approaches.

Provides rigorous, novel theoretical analysis of invariant ridge regression under non-invariant (anisotropic) data distributions in both under- and over-parameterized regimes, showing precise conditions (correlation between invariant/non-invariant features, degrees of freedom ratios) under which test-time symmetrization or data augmentation can hurt generalization even when the ground-truth function is truly invariant. The theory is carefully derived using deterministic equivalents/random matrix theory and validated with simulations that match predictions closely.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation across many benchmark datasets (MNIST, ModelNet40, QM9, QM7b, rMD17, OC20, and even an LLM materials dataset), consistently revealing surprisingly high levels of canonicalization/distributional symmetry breaking that is not widely appreciated in the community.

Interesting, non-trivial, and somewhat counter-intuitive empirical finding that despite high canonicalization, augmentation/equivariance still helps on molecular datasets (QM9/QM7b) but hurts on ModelNet40/MNIST, motivating further mechanistic investigation (task-dependent metric, locality experiments) rather than just reporting the anomaly.

Very thorough supplementary material: ablations on architecture size (showing metric robustness), p-value computation and calibration, interpretability analysis of the learned classifier decision boundary (Mollweide projections, PCA of embeddings, instability analysis), and multiple sanity checks (rotated/canonicalized synthetic controls) that reinforce the validity of the proposed metric.
The paper is honest about limitations of its secondary contribution (the task-dependent metric), explicitly showing architecture sensitivity and inconclusive results rather than overselling it.
weaknesses: The central empirical puzzle raised by the paper (why augmentation helps QM9/QM7b despite canonicalization but hurts ModelNet40/MNIST) is not conclusively resolved; the locality hypothesis (Section 5.3) is only suggestive/correlational and the paper itself acknowledges the causal link is hard to establish.

The task-dependent metric (Appendix B), while conceptually appealing, is shown to be highly sensitive to canonicalization/classifier architecture choices (Tables 2-3) and gives inconclusive results on most real datasets other than the synthetic swiss roll and toy MNIST cases, limiting its practical utility as claimed.

Models used for the regression/classification benchmarking experiments (Graphormer-style transformer, basic e3nn networks) are not state-of-the-art for these datasets, so absolute MAE/accuracy numbers may not reflect what would happen with more competitive modern architectures (e.g., Equiformer, MACE-level models), somewhat limiting the generalizability of the practical augmentation-helps/hurts conclusions.

The classifier-based metric's dependence on the choice of architecture/capacity, while shown to be fairly robust in ablations for QM9 (Table 6), is not systematically stress-tested across all datasets, and the theoretical claim that the metric approaches ideal accuracy assumes infinite samples and perfect optimization, which may not hold uniformly across the very different dataset sizes studied.

The paper's main claims rely on a fairly large and complex set of experiments/theory bundled together (a metric, ridge regression theory, and multiple dataset case studies plus a task-dependent metric); while impressively thorough, this breadth sometimes comes at the cost of depth in fully explaining any single counter-intuitive result, and the paper's narrative arc (many partially resolved open questions) may leave readers wanting a more unified take-away message.

Some presentation issues remain, e.g., minor formatting artifacts (stray text like 'this' and 'behavior' appearing oddly split across a page break near Table 1/Figure discussion), which could be polished for the camera-ready version.

strengths: Introduces a simple, interpretable, and architecture-robust two-sample classifier metric m(pX) for quantifying distributional symmetry breaking, with clean theoretical interpretation (optimal Bayes accuracy under finite-orbit models) and extensive ablations showing robustness to model size/dataset size.

Provides a genuinely novel theoretical analysis of invariant ridge regression under non-invariant data distributions, extending Elesedy & Zaidi (2021) to both under- and over-parameterized regimes, showing (counter to common intuition) that data augmentation/symmetrization can hurt even for truly invariant ground-truth functions; theory is carefully derived with deterministic equivalents from random matrix theory and validated in simulation (Figure 3).

Very broad and thorough empirical study across many real-world domains (QM9, QM7b, rMD17, OC20, ModelNet40, MNIST, an LLM materials dataset), consistently revealing surprisingly high distributional symmetry breaking, which is a valuable empirical finding for the community.

Introduces a complementary task-dependent metric t(pX,Y) that helps explain why augmentation sometimes helps despite symmetry breaking (task-irrelevant canonicalization) and sometimes hurts (task-relevant canonicalization, e.g. constructed QM7b dipole experiment, ModelNet40), producing a coherent, actionable practical flowchart (Figure 6).

Strong reproducibility effort: detailed appendices with architecture/training details, p-value computation via permutation tests, comparison to MMD with multiple kernels validating that the classifier-based metric agrees with alternative distance measures, and a public codebase.

Interesting follow-up investigations (local QM9/ModelNet40 neighborhoods, interpretability of the learned classifier's decision boundary via Mollweide projections, selective augmentation proof-of-concept) that add depth and open promising directions.
weaknesses: The task-dependent detection metric dclass(c(x), f(x)) is shown in the appendix to be quite sensitive to the choice of canonicalization network and classifier architecture (Table 6/7), undermining confidence in this variant; the paper pivots to the direct-prediction metric t(pX,Y) partly for this reason, but the latter's dependence on the quality/naturalness of the chosen canonicalization function c(·) is still a source of potential bias not fully resolved.

The theoretical results are derived in a fairly stylized linear/ridge-regression setting with a specific 'minimal model' covariance structure (coupling modes with equal strength superpositions); while illuminating, the link between this idealized theory and the complex real datasets studied empirically is largely qualitative/suggestive rather than rigorously connected (e.g., no direct estimation of correlation strength or γc for QM9/ModelNet40 to confirm the theory's regime applies).

Some central explanatory claims (e.g., that local equivariance/motif symmetry explains why augmentation helps on QM9 despite global canonicalization) are explicitly acknowledged as hypotheses needing further validation, and the paper relies on indirect evidence (lower local m(pX)) rather than a controlled causal test.

The core classifier-based metric, while interpretable, is fundamentally a lower bound/approximation to a true distributional distance, and its numeric value is entangled with the capacity/generalization behavior of the chosen classifier family (acknowledged in Appendix B), which could limit precise comparability of m(pX) values across datasets of very different modality (point clouds vs. text vs. images).

The regression benchmarks intentionally use non-state-of-the-art architectures (older Graphormer, smaller e3nn models) to isolate the augmentation effect; while justified, this limits the direct practical takeaway for state-of-the-art model design and leaves open whether findings hold for stronger models.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and under-examined question: the implicit assumption of distributional symmetry (p(x)≈p(gx)) underlying most theory and practice of equivariant learning and data augmentation.

Extensive empirical scope: the paper applies its metric to a large and diverse set of benchmarks (QM9, QM7b, ModelNet40, MNIST, rMD17, OC20, an LLM materials dataset), consistently finding non-trivial symmetry breaking, which is a useful empirical contribution to the community.

The theoretical analysis of ridge regression under non-invariant covariance (Theorems 1–2, bias-variance decompositions in both under- and over-parameterized regimes) is a non-trivial technical contribution that generalizes prior work (Elesedy & Zaidi) to the non-invariant setting.
Thorough appendix with ablations (architecture, sample size, hyperparameters), p-value/significance analysis against MMD baselines, and a reasonably detailed reproducibility statement.
The 'local motif' experiments and task-dependent metric provide an interesting attempt to explain the puzzling empirical finding that augmentation helps on QM9 despite high canonicalization.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution (m(pX) as a classifier two-sample test) is essentially a direct, fairly standard application of existing classifier two-sample test methodology (Lopez-Paz & Oquab, 2017) to a new problem framing, rather than a novel technique; the conceptual novelty is therefore limited even though the application is reasonable.

The task-dependent metric t(pX,Y) (and its variant dclass) is admitted by the authors to be architecture-sensitive and somewhat ad hoc — Table 6/7 show large swings in accuracy (69–89%) purely from canonicalization-network depth/width choices, undermining confidence in its reliability as a diagnostic tool.

The connection between the linear ridge-regression theory (Section 4) and the actual deep-learning experiments (graph transformers, e3nn) is asserted only qualitatively; there is no direct empirical verification that the specific mechanisms identified in the linear theory (correlation between invariant/non-invariant features, over- vs under-parameterization) are what actually explain the observed QM9 vs. ModelNet40 discrepancy.

The central practical takeaway (Figure 6 flowchart) is a coarse, non-quantitative heuristic ('use caution') rather than an actionable, well-calibrated decision rule, despite the paper's stated goal of providing practical diagnostic guidance.

Key explanatory hypotheses (e.g., 'local equivariance' explaining why augmentation still helps on canonicalized QM9) are explicitly acknowledged as unproven/correlational ('challenging to establish a causal link'), leaving the paper's most interesting puzzle largely unresolved.

Regression baselines are dated and explicitly non-state-of-the-art (2021-era Graphormer, small e3nn models), and results are averaged over only 3 seeds, which combined with the very large number of dataset/property/augmentation-setting combinations tested raises concerns about statistical robustness of some fine-grained comparisons (e.g., Table 4's many properties).

The paper is very broad (two metrics, extensive theory, ten+ datasets, several appendices), which dilutes focus; the narrative reads as a large collection of loosely connected exploratory findings rather than a tightly unified contribution with a clear, generalizable conclusion.

strengths: Introduces a simple, interpretable, model-agnostic diagnostic (m(pX)) based on a two-sample classifier test to quantify distributional symmetry breaking, sidestepping the kernel-selection issues of prior non-parametric tests (Chiu & Bloem-Reddy).

Provides a rigorous theoretical analysis of invariant ridge regression under non-invariant covariance, in both under- and over-parameterized regimes, using deterministic equivalents/random matrix theory, showing precisely when data augmentation and test-time symmetrization help or hurt even for truly invariant ground-truth functions.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation across many benchmark domains (QM9, QM7b, ModelNet40, MNIST, rMD17, OC20, and an LLM materials dataset), consistently uncovering surprisingly high degrees of symmetry bias.

Uncovers a genuinely interesting and non-obvious empirical pattern: despite high symmetry bias in nearly all datasets, augmentation/equivariance helps in molecular property prediction (QM9/QM7b) but hurts in ModelNet40/MNIST, motivating further mechanistic investigation (task-dependent metric, locality analysis).

Proposes a complementary task-dependent metric t(pX,Y) and a locality analysis (local QM9/ModelNet40) that together provide a coherent, actionable explanation (and practical flowchart) for when equivariant methods are likely to help or hurt.

Very thorough supplementary material: ablations over architecture/hyperparameters showing robustness of the task-independent metric, p-value/MMD comparisons validating the classifier-based metric against alternative distances, and interpretability analysis of the trained classifier (Mollweide visualizations, instability analysis).

Formal proof (Section A.1) that gradient descent on equivariant networks under invariant loss is agnostic to per-datapoint orientation, providing clean theoretical motivation for why equivariant methods discard orientation information.
weaknesses: The task-dependent metric t(pX,Y) is comparatively ad hoc, depends on an arbitrary choice of canonicalization network c(·), and the appendix ablations (Table 6/7) show non-trivial sensitivity to network architecture, which somewhat undercuts its reliability as a diagnostic.

The connection between the ridge-regression theory (Section 4) and the deep-learning experiments (Section 5) is more qualitative/motivational than quantitatively predictive; the theory does not directly explain the specific QM9-vs-ModelNet40 discrepancy that is the empirical centerpiece of the paper.

Some central empirical puzzles (why equivariance still helps on already highly-canonicalized QM9) remain only partially explained via the locality hypothesis, which itself relies on a somewhat heuristic measure (predicting g from gx) and is left as future work.

The paper is very dense, combining two metrics, multiple theoretical regimes, and many datasets; the core narrative could be more tightly focused, and some results (e.g., selective augmentation in D.2.4) are only preliminary proofs of concept.

Baseline equivariant/non-equivariant architectures used for the regression tasks are not state-of-the-art (explicitly acknowledged by the authors), limiting the strength of practical conclusions about equivariant method performance.

The classifier-based metric's theoretical interpretation (Section B) relies on generic learning-theoretic bounds that are not particularly tight or specific to this setting, leaving the precise meaning of m(pX) somewhat informal for infinite groups.
